B11_00: The cellular response to salt stress covers adjustments defending volume and ion balance when extracellular salt changes, mattering most in the kidney medulla. Aldose reductase makes sorbitol as a compatible osmolyte, aquaporin-1 allows water flux, a potassium-chloride cotransporter and the sodium pump gamma subunit tune ions, and TRPV4 reports swelling. Mitochondrial calcium components, LETM1, transcript-stability and DNA-repair factors handle hypertonic damage.
B11_01: The cellular response to nitrosative stress comprises adaptations following protein S-nitrosylation, nitration and DNA damage from nitric oxide or peroxynitrite, mattering most in inflamed tissue and neurons where glial nitric oxide drives neurodegeneration. PARK7/DJ-1 is a redox-sensitive protector whose loss causes early-onset parkinsonism, DNAJA1 chaperones modified proteins, ATG5 autophagy clears damage, ATM signals DNA lesions, and DDIT3/CHOP commits cells to apoptosis.
B11_02: The cellular response to hydroperoxide is how cells sense lipid- and membrane-derived hydroperoxides and alter gene expression, redox output, survival signalling or growth arrest, setting the threshold between tolerated stress and oxidant-driven death. It is relevant to atherosclerosis, where oxidised lipoproteins taken up via CD36 deliver oxidants. Membrane glutathione transferase detoxifies, p53-induced genes bias outcome, PRKCD and DAPK1 transduce death signals, and corepressors reprogram transcription.
B11_03: These mechanisms hold off cellular senescence, the permanent cell cycle exit triggered by telomere erosion, oncogene activation or persistent damage. Telomerase components TERT and TERC with protective TERF2 keep chromosome ends from reading as damage, SIRT1 and SIRT6 restrain stress responses at chromatin, BCL6, TBX2 and TWIST1 repress the p16/p21 programme, and CDK6 and microRNAs sustain proliferation. Loss causes ageing; excess lets damaged cells escape the senescence barrier.
B11_04: Stress-induced premature senescence is the irreversible cell cycle exit after oxidative or genotoxic insult such as hydrogen peroxide or irradiation. It limits propagation of damaged genomes and blocks tumour formation, yet accumulated arrested cells drive ageing phenotypes and chronic inflammation. Signals pass through p38 MAPK and its downstream kinase to p53, which induces p21; SIRT1 restrains p53, a secreted WNT shapes the paracrine phenotype, and a circadian factor contributes.
B11_05: The cellular response to leucine starvation is how cells stand down anabolism when this growth-licensing amino acid runs short. With leucine present, sestrins release GATOR2 and Rag GTPases let mTORC1 dock at the lysosome; on withdrawal mTORC1 falls, protein synthesis declines and autophagy recovers amino acids. Uncharged tRNA drives an ATF4 and ATF2 arm inducing transporters, synthetases and sestrins, coupling nutrient supply to cell size, muscle balance and immune activation.
B11_06: Cells respond to hyperoxia with stress signalling, antioxidant and clearance responses, and death when damage exceeds repair, mattering most in lungs of preterm infants and ventilated patients, where oxygen injures alveolar epithelium and endothelium in bronchopulmonary dysplasia and acute lung injury. Reactive species rise with NADPH oxidase activity, FOXO1 redirects expression toward stress resistance and apoptosis, FAS commits damaged cells to death, ATG7 autophagy clears oxidised cargo, and caveolin-1 contributes.
B11_07: The cellular hyperosmotic response is how shrinking cells sense water loss and restore volume and ionic balance, mattering most in the kidney medulla; failure leaves concentrated salt, protein damage and DNA breaks. WNK1 and WNK3 activate OXSR1 and STK39 to drive cation-chloride transport, while NFAT5 induces osmolyte machinery including aldose reductase for sorbitol. Aquaporin water flux, glucose uptake, mitochondrial ion handling and ARHGEF2 cytoskeletal remodelling accompany it.
B11_08: These braking mechanisms block hypoxia-induced intrinsic apoptosis so cells survive ischaemia, limiting infarct size in heart, brain and kidney while letting hypoxic tumour cells persist and resist therapy. PI3K and MEK signalling sustains anti-apoptotic gene expression, an ARC-type inhibitor blocks caspase activation, an ER chaperone and a transmembrane BAX inhibitor buffer calcium release and mitochondrial permeabilisation, PINK1 maintains mitochondrial integrity, and glycolytic adaptation supports survival.
B11_09: This covers how cells sense hydrogen peroxide, both metabolic by-product and second messenger, with outcomes from restored redox balance to inflammation, arrest and regulated death in ageing, ischaemia-reperfusion and neurodegeneration. Catalase, thioredoxin and PARK7 buffer the signal, NFE2L2 drives antioxidant transcription, and SRC, ABL1, PRKCD and MAP3K5 relay it, RELA linking it to IL6 and TRPM2 and TRPA1 to calcium. Excess damage engages autophagy, permeability transition and necroptosis.
B11_10: The glucose starvation response switches cells from biosynthesis to conservation and self-digestion, preserving ATP during ischaemia, exercise and nutrient-poor tumour microenvironments. Falling energy charge activates AMP-activated kinase, restraining anabolic signalling and licensing autophagy via the beclin 1, VPS34 and ATG14 complex. PERK-driven ATF4 induces amino-acid supply enzymes, sestrins, FOXO3, p53 and SIRT1 reinforce catabolic programmes, and transporters, GATOR/KICSTOR components and perilipins tie sensing to mTORC1 and fuel stores.
B11_11: These inputs amplify the hypoxic response, making metabolic, survival and transcriptional remodelling stronger or longer-lasting than the oxygen signal alone, which matters in ischaemic tissue, hypoxic tumour cores and pulmonary and neuronal adaptation. The genes are heterogeneous: a de novo DNA methyltransferase links hypoxia to epigenetic reprogramming, a two-pore potassium channel and a metabotropic glutamate receptor connect excitability to oxygen stress, and two microRNAs tune downstream transcripts.
B11_12: These inputs push damaged, stressed or oncogene-activated cells into senescence, a permanent cell cycle exit that blocks tumour formation, as mutant KRAS triggers arrest rather than transformation, while chronic activation drives ageing and inflammatory secretion. TP53 is central with effectors YPEL3 and PAWR and CGAS sensing of cytosolic DNA giving an interferon-flavoured arrest; MIR34A, MIR22 and SIRT1 tune the response, yielding durable arrest with altered secretion and immune visibility.
B11_13: The cellular hypotonic response is how swelling cells sense water uptake and restore volume before membrane or cytoskeletal damage, mattering for epithelial secretion, corneal transparency, renal water handling and nociception; component loss causes corneal dystrophy and neuropathy. TRPV4 and aquaporins detect stretch and dilution, CLCN2 and SLC12A6 export solutes for regulatory volume decrease, WNK-activated OXSR1, STK39 and CAB39 set cotransporter phosphorylation, and myosin light chain kinase adjusts tension.
B11_14: These braking mechanisms keep cells alive when oxidative hydrogen peroxide would push them into programmed death, mattering for cardiomyocytes after ischaemia, dopaminergic neurons and regenerating tissue. MET survival signalling converges on AKT1 to suppress apoptosis, while RACK1 and the mitochondrial chaperone TRAP1 restrain death machinery. PARK7 and PINK1, mutated in recessive parkinsonism, protect mitochondria; miR-21, miR-17/92 and let-7 tune survival, and carbonic anhydrase 3 buffers oxidants in muscle.
B11_15: These controls set how readily hydrogen peroxide permeabilizes mitochondria and commits a cell to death, deciding whether a peroxide burst is buffered or converted into caspase activation, which matters for neuronal survival and ischaemic tolerance. Most components brake: AKT1 promotes survival, PARK7 and PINK1 protect mitochondria and their loss causes recessive Parkinson's disease, TRAP1 restrains permeabilization, RACK1 scaffolds kinases, carbonic anhydrase III buffers thiols, and two microRNAs tune it.
B11_16: These inputs tip accumulating hydrogen peroxide from detoxification toward death, raising the rate and extent of peroxide-triggered programmed cell death, which matters in ischaemia-reperfusion injury, neurodegeneration and cardiomyocyte loss. FOXO3 drives pro-apoptotic and redox genes, PAWR acts as a pro-apoptotic effector partner, and mitochondrial endonuclease G fragments nuclear DNA caspase-independently. A microRNA and a forkhead repressor add tuning, so sensitivity reflects gene expression as much as oxidant burden.
B11_17: Because zinc is a cofactor for hundreds of enzymes and transcription factors, cells monitor its availability and remodel transport and transcription when it runs short. Intestinal uptake depends on SLC39A4, whose loss causes acrodermatitis enteropathica with dermatitis, diarrhoea and impaired growth, while SLC39A5 handles serosal zinc and is linked to myopia. SP1 and FOS then alter targets including osteocalcin and RANK, connecting zinc to bone, epithelial integrity and immunity.
B11_18: Osmosensory signaling is the route from changed external osmolarity to a corrective response before cells swell or shrink past tolerance, mattering for water balance, blood pressure and thirst and vasopressin responses. Mechanosensitive TRPV channels admit calcium, the WNK-OXSR1 module phosphorylates cation-chloride cotransporters to move ions and water, and a sodium-sensing channel subunit contributes. Osmotic stress also activates NLRP3 with ASC and caspase-1, linking volume change to interleukin-1.
B11_19: Oncogene-induced senescence is the permanent proliferative arrest some cells adopt instead of transformation after a lesion such as mutant HRAS. Driver-bearing cells withdraw irreversibly, adopt a flattened secretory phenotype and are often cleared immunologically, so its loss marks progression from benign lesion to carcinoma. Inhibitors including p21 enforce arrest, PML bodies organise signalling, HMGA proteins build heterochromatic foci locking down proliferative genes, and lineage factors such as SPI1 reprogram transcription.
B11_20: This layer sets how strongly SREBP transcription factors drive cholesterol and fatty acid synthesis. INSIG1 and INSIG2 retain the SREBP cleavage-activating protein complex in the endoplasmic reticulum when sterols are abundant, blocking Golgi transport and proteolytic activation, while SPRING1, PAQR3 and TMED2 affect trafficking; AMFR and FBXW7 degrade the mature nuclear form. Loss drives unchecked lipogenesis and cholesterol accumulation, linking this to steatosis, hyperlipidaemia and tumour lipid supply.
